subject: Pathology
vignette: A 63-year-old man with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis presents with progressive lower extremity edema, proteinuria of 6 g per 24 hours, and hypoalbuminemia. Renal biopsy shows glomerular deposition of amorphous pink material. Special staining produces red-orange deposits on nonpolarized light and apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
question: Which of the following best identifies the amyloid fibril protein in this patient?

options.text: AL, derived from immunoglobulin light chains
AA, a serum amyloid A protein
Beta-2 microglobulin
Beta-amyloid protein from amyloid precursor protein
Transthyretin

explanation_correct: Secondary amyloidosis is caused by AA fibrils derived from serum amyloid A protein, and it is the form seen with chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, familial Mediterranean fever, and protracted infection. Amyloid is extracellular protein deposited in an abnormal fibrillar beta-pleated sheet configuration, and renal involvement classically produces nephrotic syndrome, exactly as in this patient. Congo red staining shows red-orange deposits on nonpolarized light and classic apple-green birefringence when polarized.

explanation_incorrect.A: AL fibrils from immunoglobulin light chains cause primary amyloidosis, which is associated with plasma cell dyscrasias such as multiple myeloma rather than with chronic inflammation.
explanation_incorrect.B: Beta-2 microglobulin causes dialysis-related amyloidosis in patients with end-stage renal disease on long-term dialysis, and this patient has chronic inflammatory arthritis rather than dialysis dependence.
explanation_incorrect.C: Beta-amyloid protein cleaved from amyloid precursor protein is deposited in the brain in Alzheimer disease, producing amyloid plaques and dementia rather than nephrotic syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Transthyretin amyloidosis is either the sporadic wild-type form associated with aging and mainly affecting the heart, or a hereditary mutant form causing familial amyloid polyneuropathy and cardiomyopathy.

educationalObjective: Secondary amyloidosis from chronic inflammation such as rheumatoid arthritis is caused by AA fibrils derived from serum amyloid A, and renal deposition typically produces nephrotic syndrome.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 69-year-old man presents with an enlarged tongue that he cannot protrude past his teeth, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, firm waxy thickening of the skin with easy bruising, and progressive dyspnea from a restrictive cardiomyopathy on echocardiography. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation reveal a monoclonal band, and bone marrow biopsy shows a clonal plasma cell population.
question: Which of the following best identifies the cause of his symptoms?

options.text: AA amyloid fibrils from chronic inflammation
Islet amyloid polypeptide deposition in pancreatic islets
AL amyloidosis in association with a plasma cell dyscrasia
Beta-2 microglobulin deposition from long-term dialysis
Calcitonin amyloid in medullary thyroid carcinoma

explanation_correct: Primary amyloidosis is produced by AL fibrils derived from immunoglobulin light chains and occurs in plasma cell dyscrasias such as multiple myeloma, which this patient's monoclonal band and clonal marrow population indicate. Amyloid deposition causes organ-specific manifestations: macroglossia and carpal tunnel syndrome in the musculoskeletal system, waxy skin thickening with easy bruising, and restrictive cardiomyopathy in the heart, along with nephrotic syndrome or hepatosplenomegaly elsewhere. Amyloid is an extracellular beta-pleated sheet protein that shows apple-green birefringence with Congo red under polarized light.

explanation_incorrect.B: AA fibrils arise from serum amyloid A in chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease, not from immunoglobulin light chains in a plasma cell dyscrasia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Islet amyloid polypeptide is amylin deposited in pancreatic islets in type 2 diabetes mellitus, producing glucose intolerance rather than macroglossia and restrictive cardiomyopathy.
explanation_incorrect.D: Beta-2 microglobulin amyloid occurs in patients on long-term dialysis for end-stage renal disease and typically involves bone and joints, not this presentation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Calcitonin amyloid is localized to medullary thyroid carcinoma and is secreted by the tumor cells themselves, so it does not explain systemic deposition in the tongue, skin, and heart.

educationalObjective: AL amyloidosis from immunoglobulin light chains occurs with plasma cell dyscrasias such as multiple myeloma and produces macroglossia, carpal tunnel syndrome, skin changes, and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 74-year-old man with end-stage renal disease has been on hemodialysis three times weekly for 14 years. He develops bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome and destructive cystic bone lesions in the wrists and shoulders. Biopsy of the synovium and bone lesions shows amyloid deposits.
question: Which of the following best identifies the fibril protein responsible for this patient's disease?

options.text: Beta-2 microglobulin
Serum amyloid A
Transthyretin
Immunoglobulin light chains
Atrial natriuretic peptide

explanation_correct: Dialysis-related amyloidosis is caused by beta-2 microglobulin deposition and occurs in patients with end-stage renal disease on long-term dialysis, as in this patient with 14 years of hemodialysis. The deposits favor bone and joint structures, producing carpal tunnel syndrome and characteristic cystic bone lesions. As with all amyloid, the deposits can be identified by Congo red staining, which shows red-orange material on nonpolarized light and apple-green birefringence under polarized light.

explanation_incorrect.A: Serum amyloid A produces AA fibrils in secondary amyloidosis from chronic inflammation such as rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease, not in dialysis patients.
explanation_incorrect.B: Transthyretin amyloidosis is the aging-associated wild-type form that mainly affects the heart or the hereditary mutant form causing polyneuropathy and cardiomyopathy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Immunoglobulin light chains form AL amyloid in primary amyloidosis associated with plasma cell dyscrasias, whereas this patient's disease is dialysis related.
explanation_incorrect.E: Atrial natriuretic peptide forms isolated atrial amyloidosis associated with aging and an increased risk of atrial fibrillation, not the bone and joint lesions of long-term dialysis.

educationalObjective: Dialysis-related amyloidosis in end-stage renal disease on long-term dialysis is caused by beta-2 microglobulin deposition, classically producing carpal tunnel syndrome and bone and joint disease.

subject: Pathology
vignette: An 82-year-old woman dies of progressive heart failure with echocardiographic features of a restrictive cardiomyopathy. At autopsy, the myocardium shows amorphous pink deposits on H&E staining that fail to stain with Congo red in the expected fashion on nonpolarized light but show apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Mass spectrometry of the deposits identifies a normal-sequence transport protein rather than a mutant or immunoglobulin protein. She had no history of chronic infection or myeloma.
question: Which of the following best describes the probable type of amyloid in this patient?

options.text: Hereditary amyloidosis from a mutated transthyretin sequence
Sporadic wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis associated with aging
Secondary amyloidosis from protracted infection
Localized calcitonin amyloid of the heart
Beta-amyloid protein deposition within cardiac myocytes

explanation_correct: Transthyretin amyloidosis has two forms: the sporadic wild-type TTR form, which is slowly progressive, associated with aging, and mainly affects the heart, and the hereditary mutated TTR form, which causes familial amyloid polyneuropathy and cardiomyopathy. Amyloid produces a restrictive cardiomyopathy, and deposits are identified by Congo red with apple-green birefringence under polarized light. This patient's advanced age, isolated cardiac disease, absence of a family history or plasma cell dyscrasia, and normal-sequence protein all favor the wild-type, aging-associated form.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis requires a mutation and typically presents with familial amyloid polyneuropathy and cardiomyopathy in younger patients with an affected family, whereas the protein here is normal sequence.
explanation_incorrect.C: Secondary amyloidosis from protracted infection is due to serum amyloid A fibrils and occurs with chronic inflammatory states; this patient has neither infection nor the AA protein.
explanation_incorrect.D: Calcitonin amyloid is localized to medullary thyroid carcinoma and is secreted by tumor cells, so it would not explain isolated cardiac deposition in an elderly woman.
explanation_incorrect.E: Beta-amyloid is cleaved from amyloid precursor protein and deposits in the brain in Alzheimer disease; it is not the cardiac amyloid found here.

educationalObjective: Wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis is a sporadic, aging-associated, slowly progressive form that mainly affects the heart and causes restrictive cardiomyopathy.
